## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes linked to land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation, however, but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their cumulative impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@oliver2014interactions; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number]. Given these complexities, forecasting changes to biodiversity exposed to multiple global change drivers will require an understanding of the mechanisms underlying the multifactorial nature of global change drivers.

A growing body of literature shows that single and multiple global change drivers affect community biomass, plant community composition and diversity in grasslands, assuming that the main underlying mechanisms for changes in diversity is competition for nutrients and light [@borer2014herbivores; @li2024water; @harpole2016addition; @klein2004experimental; @collins2022global], with few exceptions where this specific mechanism is tested [@eskelinen2022light]. Warming and nitrogen addition typically increase community biomass (@fig-concept a), which can thus shift the intensity and nature of the dominant plant-plant interactions. Specifically, this may lead to communities with taller, faster growing species which are stronger competitors, especially for light [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. Grazing removes community biomass [@frank2005interactive; @Bernes2015-yg], while also nutrients from urine and dung, and so impacts on community biomass are variable but can lead to increased diversity, particularly in more productive habitats [@Austrheim2001-nu; @frank2005interactive; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @borer2024planning; @proulx1998reversal]. Thus, grazing has been shown to reverse the effects of warming and nitrogen addition preventing species loss [@kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @klein2004experimental; @borer2014herbivores; @post2008opposing; @song2020grazing]. While these studies suggest a change in the magnitude of competition for resources, the mechanisms that different global change drivers are mediated through community biomass has rarely been tested in a unified way within a single experiment. @white2014direct studied direct and indirect effect of plant diversity in three temperate grasslands and identified shoot biomass a key indirect driver of species loss in response to grazing and precipitation. @Vandvik2020-hu showed that complex interactions of environmental drivers could be reduced by including biomass as a proxy of plant-plant interactions. We therefore propose that we could generalize the effects of multiple global change drivers by using community biomass as a *common currency*, which reflects the magnitude of their impacts on competitive interactions. If so, knowing the general patterns and trends in community biomass could predict changes in plant biodiversity without testing the direct effects of different global change drivers (@fig-concept).

![Two alternative hypotheses for how three global change drivers warming, nitrogen addition and clipping (or grazing) affect plant diversity. a) Warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping (or grazing) affect diversity directly, or b) these drivers affect diversity indirectly, mediated through community biomass as a *common currency*.](figures/Figure1_hypotheses.png){#fig-concept width="600"}

We test this prediction with a global change experiment in mountain grasslands, because they harbor unique biodiversity and provide important ecosystem functions and services such as carbon sequestration, water cycling, and grazing pastures; underpinning the lives and livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people [@egan2017mountain]. We manipulate three common global change drivers in a field experiment: climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping or natural grazing (@fig-methods).

Plant community responses to global change drivers often differ along environmental gradients and across habitats because effects can be direct or indirect and responses can be non-linear [@milchunas1993quantitative; @elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @delnevo2018plastic; @Vandvik2020-hu]. To assess the degree of context-dependency and how community responses are mediated through community biomass, we repeated the experiment in two different environments, an alpine and a sub-alpine grassland community in Western Norway. Montane grasslands in Norway are transhumance-based grazing systems [@reinton1955seter; @austad2004overview], grazed by domestic and natural grazers with the extant grazing pressure decreasing with elevation [@halbritter2025effects; @halbritter2025data]. The two sites represent different annual and growing season temperatures, with the alpine site being more temperature and nutrient limited (Supplementary Figures S1). By replicating the experiment in two different environmental contexts we can test the generality of our hypothesis [@fraser2013coordinated].

We hypothesize that these global change drivers affect diversity and species composition mediated through community biomass, resulting in a change in competitive interactions, but alternative mechanisms are possible. For example, some species may be physiologically intolerant of very high or low temperature and therefore go locally extinct or successfully colonize, regardless of the competitive environment (REFs). Second, increased nitrogen addition, especially at high levels, can lead to acidic soil conditions [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity due to differences in tolerance to acidic conditions, independently of competitive interactions. Similarly, some species may be particularly tolerant or intolerant to direct effects of grazing irrespective of competitive interactions [@archibald2019unified]. Such shifts in species composition might therefore not be mediated through community biomass. Ecological indicator values can be used to describe species community composition in response to environmental affinities and can provide further insights into the mechanisms of these dynamics [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range].

Here we exposed montane grassland communities in Western Norway, replicated across two sites, to three global change drivers using a split-plot design (@fig-methods). Plant communities were transplanted to lower elevation to simulate warmer climate. We fertilized the communities using seven levels ranging between 0 and 100 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^, and simulated grazing by clipping at two different intensities and had one natural grazing treatment. After three years of global change treatments, we harvested community biomass at peak growing season and assessed the change in vascular plant species composition and diversity.
